title: Wireless Security Basics
summary: Learn why Wi-Fi needs special protection, how WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 differ, how the 4-way handshake creates encryption keys, and which common wireless threats and defenses appear on the CCST Cybersecurity exam.
objectives: Explain why wireless networks are harder to secure than wired networks
Compare WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 and their Personal and Enterprise modes
Describe the WPA2/WPA3 4-way handshake and the keys it produces
Identify common wireless threats such as rogue access points and evil twins

blocks.markdown:
A coffee-shop owner sets up Wi-Fi for staff and uses the same password for the point-of-sale tablets and the guest network. The signal reaches the car park. Months later, card data is stolen — someone sat outside, joined the network with the shared password and quietly watched the traffic.

With a wired network an attacker needs physical access to a port. With wireless, **the radio signal is the cable**, and it passes through walls to anyone within range. That is why Wi-Fi needs strong authentication, strong encryption and careful design. The CCST Cybersecurity exam expects you to know the security protocols, the threats and the basic defenses.

## Wireless building blocks

- **Access point (AP)** — the device that bridges wireless clients onto the wired network. In enterprises, APs are often managed by a **wireless LAN controller (WLC)**.
- **SSID** — the network name a client connects to. Hiding the SSID is **not** a security control: the name still appears in client probe requests and is easily discovered.
- **Station / client** — a laptop, phone or IoT device that associates to an AP.
- **802.11** — the IEEE family of Wi-Fi standards (Wi-Fi 4/5/6/6E/7). **802.11i** defines the security that became WPA2.

Two security jobs must be done before data flows:

1. **Authentication** — is this device or user allowed on the network?
2. **Encryption** — protect every frame over the air so that it cannot be read or altered.

## From WEP to WPA3

| Protocol | Year | Encryption | Status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **WEP** | 1999 | RC4 with a short 24-bit IV | **Broken** — can be cracked in minutes; never use |
| **WPA** | 2003 | TKIP (RC4-based stop-gap) | Deprecated |
| **WPA2** | 2004 | AES-**CCMP** | Still widely used; acceptable with a strong passphrase or Enterprise mode |
| **WPA3** | 2018 | AES-CCMP / **GCMP-256**, SAE, mandatory PMF | Current recommendation |

### Personal vs. Enterprise

| Mode | How users authenticate | Best for |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Personal (PSK / SAE)** | One shared passphrase for everyone | Homes, very small offices |
| **Enterprise (802.1X)** | Each user or device has its own credentials, checked by a **RADIUS** server using **EAP** (e.g. EAP-TLS, PEAP) | Businesses |

With **WPA2-Personal**, anyone who captures a handshake can try to guess the passphrase *offline*, so a weak passphrase can be cracked. **WPA3-Personal** replaces the PSK exchange with **SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)**, which resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy. WPA3 also makes **Protected Management Frames (PMF, 802.11w)** mandatory, which blocks forged deauthentication frames.

**Enterprise mode** is preferred in organisations: credentials are individual, revocable and logged, and with **EAP-TLS** each device authenticates with a certificate. RADIUS and AAA are explored further in [Troubleshooting AAA: TACACS+ and RADIUS](/learn/cisco-security-certification-track/troubleshooting-aaa-tacacs-plus-and-radius).

**Open networks** (no password) used to send everything in the clear. **Wi-Fi Enhanced Open (OWE)** now encrypts open networks without a password, but it does not authenticate the AP. On any public Wi-Fi, use HTTPS and a [VPN](/learn/cisco-security-certification-track/vpn-fundamentals).

## The 4-way handshake

After authentication, both the client and the AP hold a **Pairwise Master Key (PMK)**. In Personal mode the PMK comes from the passphrase (WPA2) or from SAE (WPA3); in Enterprise mode it comes from the 802.1X/EAP exchange with RADIUS. The PMK itself is never sent over the air. The **4-way handshake** proves that both sides know the PMK and derives fresh session keys:

- **PTK (Pairwise Transient Key)** — encrypts unicast traffic between this client and the AP.
- **GTK (Group Temporal Key)** — encrypts broadcast and multicast traffic, shared by all clients on the AP.

steps.label: PMK in place
steps.note: Both sides already share the PMK after authentication. It never travels over the air.

steps.label: Message 1: ANonce
steps.note: The AP sends a random number (ANonce) in the clear.

steps.label: Derive PTK
steps.detail: PTK = f(PMK, ANonce, SNonce, both MAC addresses)
steps.note: The client creates its own random SNonce and computes the PTK from the PMK, both nonces and both MAC addresses.

steps.label: Message 2: SNonce + MIC
steps.note: The client sends its SNonce with a MIC computed using the PTK. The AP derives the same PTK and checks the MIC — proving the client knows the PMK.

steps.label: Message 3: GTK (encrypted) + MIC
steps.note: The AP proves it also knows the PMK and delivers the group key (GTK), encrypted with the PTK.

steps.label: Message 4: ACK + MIC
steps.note: The client confirms that the keys are installed.

steps.label: Encrypted data (AES-CCMP/GCMP)
steps.note: Unicast frames are now protected with the PTK and broadcasts with the GTK.

steps.label: Why weak WPA2-PSK fails
steps.note: Messages 1-2 contain enough to test password guesses offline. Long random passphrases, WPA3-SAE or Enterprise mode defeat this.

blocks.markdown:
## Common wireless threats

| Threat | What happens | Defenses |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Rogue access point** | An unauthorised AP plugged into the wired network creates a back door | Wireless IDS/IPS (rogue detection on the WLC), 802.1X on switch ports, regular surveys |
| **Evil twin** | An attacker's AP imitates a real SSID to lure clients and intercept traffic | WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with server certificate validation, user training, VPN |
| **Deauthentication attack** | Forged management frames disconnect clients (DoS, or to capture a handshake) | **PMF/802.11w** (mandatory in WPA3) |
| **Offline passphrase cracking** | Guessing a WPA2-PSK from a captured handshake | Long passphrase, WPA3-SAE, Enterprise mode |
| **Eavesdropping** | Reading traffic on open or weakly encrypted networks | WPA2/WPA3, HTTPS, VPN |
| **WPS PIN attacks** | Brute-forcing the 8-digit Wi-Fi Protected Setup PIN | **Disable WPS** |
| **Jamming** | Radio interference stops all communication | Spectrum analysis, physical investigation |
| **War driving** | Searching for networks from a moving vehicle | Strong security, sensible signal coverage |

blocks.title: Myths that are not security
blocks.markdown: **Hiding the SSID** and **MAC address filtering** are often recommended, but both are easily bypassed: hidden SSIDs appear in probe requests, and MAC addresses can be observed and spoofed. Use them, if at all, only on top of WPA2/WPA3 — never instead of it.

## Wireless hardening checklist

- Use **WPA3** (or WPA2/WPA3 transition mode while old clients remain); never WEP or WPA/TKIP.
- In businesses use **802.1X Enterprise**, ideally **EAP-TLS** with certificates, and make clients validate the RADIUS server certificate.
- For Personal mode, use a long random passphrase (20+ characters) and change it when staff leave.
- Enable **Protected Management Frames**; disable **WPS**.
- **Segment** traffic: separate SSIDs and VLANs for staff, guests and IoT, with firewall rules between them (see [Firewalls and Network Filtering](/learn/cisco-security-certification-track/firewalls-and-network-filtering)). Guest networks should reach only the internet, with client isolation.
- Change default admin credentials, keep AP and controller firmware updated, and manage them over HTTPS/SSH only.
- Enable rogue AP detection and review wireless logs.
- Adjust transmit power and AP placement so coverage does not extend far beyond the building.

blocks.caption: A Linux AP (hostapd) configured for WPA3-Personal with SAE, mandatory PMF and WPS disabled.
blocks.code:
interface=wlan0
ssid=Lab-WPA3
hw_mode=g
channel=6

# RSN (WPA2/WPA3 family) only - no legacy WPA/TKIP
wpa=2
# WPA3-Personal; use "WPA-PSK SAE" for WPA2/WPA3 transition mode
wpa_key_mgmt=SAE
sae_password=<long-random-passphrase>
rsn_pairwise=CCMP
# Protected Management Frames: required
ieee80211w=2
# WPS disabled
wps_state=0

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.markdown: Match the term to the protocol: **TKIP → WPA**, **AES-CCMP → WPA2**, **SAE and mandatory PMF → WPA3**, **802.1X + RADIUS → Enterprise mode**. If a question describes an AP that copies a legitimate SSID, the answer is an **evil twin**; an unauthorised AP plugged into the LAN is a **rogue AP**.

blocks.title: Try it yourself
blocks.markdown:
Audit **your own** home or lab Wi-Fi — do not test networks you do not own or have written permission to assess.

1. Log in to your router's admin page and record: security mode (WEP/WPA2/WPA3), whether WPS is on, whether PMF is enabled, and the firmware version.
2. If supported, switch to WPA3-Personal or WPA2/WPA3 transition mode and disable WPS. Check that all your devices still connect.
3. Create a separate guest network and confirm that a guest device cannot reach your other devices (try pinging one).
4. On a laptop, run `nmcli device wifi list` (Linux) or `netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid` (Windows) and note the security of networks around you.
5. Change the router's default admin password if you have not already.

items.definition: Service Set Identifier: the name of a wireless network. Hiding it is not a security control.
Wi-Fi Protected Access 2: the 802.11i standard using AES-CCMP encryption, in Personal (PSK) or Enterprise (802.1X) mode.
The current Wi-Fi security standard, adding SAE for Personal mode, mandatory PMF and stronger Enterprise options.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: WPA3-Personal's password-based key exchange that resists offline dictionary attacks.
Port-based network access control that authenticates each user or device through EAP and a RADIUS server.
The exchange that confirms both client and AP hold the PMK and derives the PTK and delivers the GTK.
An unauthorised AP connected to an organisation's network, creating an uncontrolled entry point.
A malicious AP that imitates a legitimate SSID to trick clients into connecting to it.
Protected Management Frames: cryptographic protection for management frames such as deauthentication.

questions.question: Which encryption protocol is used by WPA2?
questions.explanation: WPA2 uses AES in CCMP mode. RC4/IV is WEP, and TKIP is the original WPA stop-gap.

questions.question: A small company wants each employee to log in to Wi-Fi with individual credentials that can be revoked when they leave. Which option fits best?
options: An open network with a hidden SSID
questions.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user or device individually through 802.1X/EAP and a RADIUS server, so access can be revoked per person.

questions.question: Which improvements does WPA3 introduce? (Choose all that apply.)
options: SAE instead of the PSK exchange
Resistance to offline dictionary attacks on the passphrase
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE, which resists offline guessing and gives forward secrecy, and makes PMF mandatory. TKIP is deprecated.

questions.question: An attacker sets up an access point broadcasting the same SSID as a hotel's Wi-Fi to intercept guests' traffic. What is this called?
questions.explanation: An evil twin impersonates a legitimate network. A rogue AP is an unauthorised AP connected to the organisation's own network.

questions.question: Which measures genuinely improve wireless security? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Placing guest and IoT devices on separate VLANs
Relying only on a hidden SSID
questions.explanation: Disabling WPS, segmentation and rogue detection all reduce risk. A hidden SSID is easily discovered and is not a security control on its own.

blocks.markdown:
## Summary

- Wireless signals reach beyond physical walls, so Wi-Fi needs strong **authentication** and **encryption**.
- **WEP** and **WPA/TKIP** are broken or deprecated. **WPA2** uses AES-CCMP; **WPA3** adds **SAE**, mandatory **PMF** and stronger options.
- **Personal** mode uses a shared passphrase; **Enterprise** mode uses **802.1X**, EAP and **RADIUS** for individual credentials.
- The **4-way handshake** proves both sides hold the PMK and derives the **PTK** (unicast) and delivers the **GTK** (broadcast).
- Watch for **rogue APs**, **evil twins**, deauthentication attacks and weak passphrases. Disable WPS, segment guests and IoT, keep firmware updated and monitor for rogues.

This completes the Network Security Basics unit. Revisit [Secure Protocols: SSL/TLS, SSH and HTTPS](/learn/cisco-security-certification-track/secure-protocols-ssl-tls-ssh-and-https) for the encryption ideas that underpin all of these defenses.
